name: Chamalal
catalog_quote: Слова могут оканчиваться как на гласный, так и на согласный. Ударение слабое динамическое, подвижное. Оно выполняет смыслоразличительную функцию. [Words may end in either a vowel or a consonant. Stress is weak, dynamic, mobile. It performs a meaning-distinguishing function.]

new_statements.quote: According to Magomedova (1981:103), stress in the Gakvari dialect of Chamalal, too, can be ‘strong’ or ‘weak’. Stress often targets the initial syllable but can appear further to the right too; long vowels do not necessarily attract stress. Initial stress can be either ‘strong’ and ‘weak’, while non-initial stress can only be ‘strong’. There are minimal pairs based on stress ‘strength’ and placement: mú:na ‘skin.INF’, mù:na ‘go.INF’; χòχa ‘bean-pod’, χoχà ‘straw’(Magomedova 2004: 27). [...] In verbs, stress tends to be initial. It shifts further to the right in causative, imperative and prohibitive forms of verbs with ‘weak’ stress on the root.
new_statements.citation: Borise, Lena. 2021. Word stress in the languages of the Caucasus. In M. Polinsky (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Languages of the Caucasus, 757-782. Oxford: OUP. (preprint lingbuzz/004203)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog_records entry (src StressTyp2, second stress) codes Chamalal as fixed initial stress. Borise reports only an initial tendency with free/contrastive placement and placement-based minimal pairs (χòχa vs χoχà, béta vs betá), i.e. a lexical, not fixed: initial syllable, system; the difference is the type (lexical (unpredictable) vs fixed: initial syllable), not just an exception list. Note the project's other catalog surface (webcat bib record) already codes the language 'lexical' from Magomedbekova 1967 ('Ударение слабое динамическое, подвижное. Оно выполняет смыслоразличительную функцию'), and Borise agrees with that coding while adding the initial tendency and the strong/weak con…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress placement is not fixed: it usually falls on the initial syllable but can fall further right, is not attracted by long vowels, and distinguishes words both by position and by a 'strong' vs 'weak' contrast (minimal pairs by placement: χòχa 'bean-pod' vs χoχà 'straw'; Bokarev's béta 'having left' vs betá 'leave.IMP', níχa 'oats' vs niχá 'take.IMP', p. 18). Verbs tend to have initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Borise notes (p. 17) that the 'strong'/'weak' distinction 'is orthogonal to that between primary and secondary stress, as both terms are used to describe the only stress in a word', and suggests strong/weak might be types of lexical pitch accent.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 18: 'strong' stress tends to stay on the same syllable through the paradigm while 'weak' stress tends to be mobile (wíha / wíhiːla / wíhabe vs basã̀ / basíːna / basã́); inflected monosyllabic roots retain stress regardless of strength; plural formants -be, -li, -e are stress-repelling while -di attracts stress (àbul / abuldí, jaʃál / jaʃaldí), with unclear cases when -di meets a strong initial stress (jéʁil / jéʁildì); stress shifts right in causative, imperative and prohibitive forms of verbs with weak root stress; Chamalal 'might have several nominal accentual classes' (uninvestigated). Borise also points to tonal analyses of Chamalal varieties (her tone chapter §2.4: Kibrik et al. 1978 and Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 posit four tones H/L/R/F for Lower Gakvari, and tones plus word stress for Gigatli, where stress lands on a syllable with R or F tone if there is one).
new_statements.identity_note: Borise's stress statement is explicitly about the Gakvari dialect of Chamalal (via Magomedova 1981, 2004 and Bokarev 1949); her companion tone chapter (lingbuzz/004204, §2.4, p. 7, also held by the project) distinguishes Lower Gakvari Chamalal (four tones, no separate stress in Kibrik & Kodzasov's account) from Gigatli Chamalal (four tones plus word stress). No statement covers the Gadyri or other dialects.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work, Borise 2021 (§6.2, pp. 17-18), describes Chamalal (Gakvari dialect) stress as free in placement with an initial tendency, contrastive by position and by 'strong'/'weak' strength, and mobile in paradigms for weak stress; this disagrees with the StressTyp2-derived catalog_records rule that puts stress fixed on the initial syllable in every word length, but agrees with the catalog's own bib-record coding 'lexical' resting on Magomedbekova 1967 (mobile, meaning-distinguishing stress) and Magomedova 1999 ('тяготеет к началу слова'). A second, source-internal disagreement is flagged by Borise herself: Kibrik et al. 1978 and Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 analyse Lower Gakvari and Gigatli Chamalal as syllable-tone systems (four tones), with word stress recognised only for Gigatli, whereas Magomedova and Bokarev give non-tonal stress accounts; Borise leaves that open ('the facts summarized in this section require further investigation').

sources.quote: 'Dialects of Chamalal have been analyzed as possessing various tonal properties, with some contradictory descriptions. Kibrik et al. (1978: 44) analyze Low Gakwari Chamalal as contrasting four tones (H, L, R, F) on the stressed syllable only, while Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 325) describe it as specifying each syllable for one of the four tones ... For Gigatli Chamalal, Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 324) postulate both a system of four tones ... and word stress. Stress targets a syllable with a R or F tone, if a word includes one. Otherwise, stress and tone are not correlated.'

sources.quote: Overview: 'Словесное ударение в дагестанских языках всегда подвижное и неавтоматическое'; Andic languages incl. Chamalal (N. Gakvari, Gigatli) analysed as syllable-tone systems (H, L, R, F), 'обычно отсутствует словесное ударение (исключение – гигатлинский диалект чамалинского)'. Gigatli §3: 'Ударение неавтоматическое, подвижное. Если в слове есть скользящий тон (R, F), то ударение, как правило, падает на него.' N. Gakvari §3: four syllable tones with many minimal pairs (has'/H слюна – has'/L жена; muna/HH шел – muna/RR свежевал), no fixed stress position stated.
